newsitem.title: USA: Encryption experts reject new US export compromise.
newsitem.headline: Encryption experts reject new US export compromise.

text.p: A compromise legislative proposal to ease strict U.S. export limits on computer encoding technology is unworkable and undesirable, leading cryptography researchers said on Wednesday.

Approved by the Senate Commerce Committee last week, the compromise bill would allow companies to export modestly strong encryption products, which scramble information and render it unreadable without a password or software "key."
But the bill would also promote the widespread adoption of encryption that allows government agencies to crack coded messages by gaining access to the software keys.
"The bill makes no sense from a technical point of view," AT&T Labs researcher Matt Blaze said. "It will be extraordinarily expensive and it won't be effective."
The Clinton administration backs strict export controls to keep strong encryption out of the hands of foreign criminals.
But since key recovery would allow government agencies to crack messages sent by criminals, the administration permits the export of strong encryption if it includes such features.

Blaze, who discovered a security flaw in the government's Clipper chip scheme in 1994, said criminals could easily evade government attempts to crack their coded messages. "The bill is not even likely to meet it's stated goals," he said.
The bill, sponsored by Arizona Republican John McCain and Nebraska Democrat Bob Kerrey, closely parallels a "trial balloon" floated by the Clinton administration in March.

The Commerce Committee passed the bill as a last minute substitute for a bill authored by Montana Republican Conrad Burns that would have virtually eliminated export controls without imposing key recovery.
Commerce Secretary William Daley urged the committee in a letter to approve the compromise instead of the Burns bill.
"We think it's a positive approach," Undersecretary of Commerce William Reinsch told Reuters Wednesday. "It helps develop a key management infrastructure and key recovery."

The Burns bill dealt only with encryption, Reinsch said. "It wasn't really a bill that was designed to help promote secure public networks," he said. "The issue of security on networks or in electronic commerce ... goes way beyond encryption."

Like the Clinton plan, the new bill would expand the government's authority to listen to coded communications. Officials would need a warrant, similiar to current law, or a subpoena to get access to keys. Access could also be granted on the basis of a foreign government's request.

"I would imagine that when people find out about this, it will be an enormously contentious issue," Kenneth Dam, law professor at the University of Chicago, said in an interview. Subpoenas can be issued in civil cases such as tax or contract disputes, said Dam, chairman of an influential National Research Council report on encryption issued last year.

Laws authorizing traditional wiretaps are more limited and can only be used after law enforcement agencies show they cannot get information through other means, Dam said. "None of those provisons apply here," he said.

Administration officials have defended their key recovery approach by arguing that they expect a decentralized array of entities to hold keys. That should be less vulnerable and less expensive than a single, giant key registry, they said.
But the infrastructure is still vulnerable even without a centralized registry, said Herbert Lin, senior staff officer with the National Academy of Science's National Research Council.
"We're not necessarily talking about a single, monolithic system," Lin said in an interview. "We're talking about a system of systems and the criticisms still apply."

The researchers were in Washington on Wednesday for a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on encryption. But senators were called away for a series of votes on the Senate floor, and the hearing was postponed until next month.
